cell.label: Patient presents with neck pain. Recent trauma?

Apply the Canadian C-spine rule. Injury with a dangerous mechanism (eg, fall from 3 ft or more or 5 stairs, diving, motor vehicle collision at >100 km/hr, rollover or ejection, or collision involving a motorized recreational vehicle or a bicycle)?
Stabilize neck; transport for immediate x-ray.

Can you safely assess range of motion of the neck (eg, simple rear-end motor vehicle collision, sitting in the office or ED, ambulatory since the injury, delayed onset of neck pain, or no midline cervical spine tenderness)?
Able to actively rotate the neck 45 degrees left and right?
No immediate x-ray needed. If pain continues, continue the evaluation.
Risk factors for fracture (eg, age 65 years or older, history of or risk factors for cancer, unexplained weight loss, or Paget's disease)?
Consider cancer: order neck x-ray and ESR.
Risk factors for infection (eg, immunosuppression, previous spine surgery, history of IV drug use, or prolonged steroid use)?
Consider osteomyelitis or septic arthritis: order CBC, ESR, white blood cell labeled bone scan, and MRI.
Weakness, numbness, and paresthesias of the arms? Reduced deep tendon reflexes?
Consider cervical disc herniation: order MRI (17% of people without symptoms have a disc herniation, so interpret with caution).
Other neurologic signs (eg, bowel or bladder dysfunction, clonus, Babinski sign, spasticity, gait disturbance, or electric shocks down the back and legs on neck flexion [Lhermitte sign])?
Consider arthritis: order x-rays, ESR, and rheumatoid factor.
Consider nonspecific neck pain without radiculopathy, cervical strain, myofascial syndrome, muscle spasm, or cervical spondylosis.
